topic: Floyd's Cycle Detection: The Tortoise and Hare Pattern
caption:
Detecting a cycle in a linked list is a classic technical interview problem.

Most beginners reach for a hash set to store visited nodes. That works, but it costs O(n) extra space.

Floyd's Cycle Detection algorithm solves this in O(1) auxiliary space using two pointers. A slow pointer moves one step at a time, while a fast pointer moves two steps.

If there is a cycle, both pointers enter the loop. With each step, the fast pointer gains exactly one node on the slow pointer, closing the gap until they inevitably collide. Because the relative distance shrinks by one each step, the slow pointer takes at most n steps before a meeting occurs.

Have you used this two-pointer pattern for other linked list problems?

topic: How Timezones and UTC are Handled in Databases
angle: This post teaches junior developers why saving timestamps in UTC is crucial and how the Postgres AT TIME ZONE command actually converts time instead of changing stored data.
caption:
Handling dates and times in distributed systems is notoriously tricky. If your database stores local time instead of UTC, you risk data corruption, inaccurate logging, and bugs during daylight saving transitions. The golden rule of backend engineering is to always persist timestamps in UTC. When using databases like PostgreSQL, commands such as AT TIME ZONE help translate those values for display rather than altering the stored truth. How do you currently handle timezones in your backend applications?

angle: Learn how prompt injection allows users to hijack an AI model's system instructions, why it is highly similar to classic SQL injection, and how developers can secure their LLM applications.
caption:
Prompt injection is one of the most critical vulnerabilities in modern AI applications.

When you build with large language models, the model consumes your system prompt and user input as a single continuous text sequence. If an attacker inputs instructions like 'ignore previous rules', the model can end up executing the user command instead of yours.

This vulnerability closely mirrors SQL injection from early web development: data and control instructions get mixed together. Defending against it requires layered security, including structured messaging formats, input sanitization, and output guardrails before triggering external actions.

Have you implemented guardrails against prompt injection in your AI projects yet?
